newsitem.title: USA: Marbles are rolling in as popular collectibles.
newsitem.headline: Marbles are rolling in as popular collectibles.

text.p: Have you lost your marbles?
If your prized collection of marbles, from, say, 40 years ago, is gathering dust in your parents' attic, you may have collectibles that some experts call a piece of Americana.
"I tell people I haven't lost them, they're just loose," laughed Cathy Runyan, proud owner of about a million marbles and author of "Knuckles Down! A Fun Guide to Marble Play."

Like most, Runyan's collection started with marbles she had as a child. Marble playing, or shooting, from the 1920s to 1940s was tops with children of all ages and it seemed everyone had a colourful bag of them, she said.
With television's arrival in the early 1950s and the start of Little League baseball, bags of marbles were put aside. Some of those old marbles today may be worth a mint.
"I would say marbles are most similar to coins in the things that make them valuable: age and condition," Runyan said. "If they're all nicked up and chewed, it's nothing."
Also, if a limited number of certain types of marbles were made, demand and value are higher, she added.
Runyan said a marble's "eye appeal, the colour or pizzaz," and size are factors that will add to its worth.

Handmade marbles -- the most coveted by collectors -- from the 1800s to World War I were mainly made in Germany. When German factories were destroyed, American machine-made marbles gained in popularity.

If your bag contains a coloured sulphide marble that has a ceramic figure in the middle, you've got something prized by most collectors. If the surrounding glass is coloured and the usually white ceramic animal or human figure inside is painted, it could be worth from $2,000 to $5,000, Runyan said.

Another collector favourite is a machine-made marble known as "Superman." Hobbyists dubbed it after the comic book hero because of its colours -- red, yellow and blue. It was made by Peltier Glass Co. of Ottawa, Ill., in the 1930s.
Marble collecting took off in the late 1980s, as adults took their childhood marbles from basements and attics, said Robert Block, author of "Marbles; Identification and Price Guide."

Block, a collector for 10 years, said early marbles did not come in sets per se, but were sold in bulk out of bins or crates. Then marketing-savvy American manufacturers began selling sets in fancy packaging, hoping they would catch on.

Marbles are often known by various names. There are swirls called Peppermint, Butterscotch, Cornhusk, Custard and Gooseberry. Others are commonly know as Sparklers, Sunbursts, Cat's and Tiger's Eyes and Conquerer.

Before you dash out to cash in your bags of old marbles, know that only the rarest command the highest prices. Your Chinese checker-type may be worth one cent, while a rare Guinea with different coloured flecks of glass in it may be worth thousands of dollars, depending on the four factors and desirability, experts say.

Block's Identification and Price Guide, written for the Marble Collectors Society of America, offers pricing examples of marbles that span the decades in condition categories of mint, near mint, good and collectible.

Of the many popular handmade swirl marbles, a solid core swirl with four bands of colour in the core, has a range of $1 for a 1/2-inch collectible, $25 for a 1 to 1-1/2 inch good marble to about $250 for a mint, two inches and larger.

A ribbon core swirl has a wide, flat band of colour in the centre of a rod that is twisted when the marble is cut off the cane. For these marbles with a single ribbon and well-formed outer layers, $500 is average for a mint condition piece, two inches and over. Even a small near mint can fetch about $110.

Perhaps you have a Joseph's Coat swirl marble. These swirls have an outer layer of glass comprised of different coloured strands placed closely together in dark, earthy colours or bright English-style colours. Collectors can expect a value range of $20 to $60 for smaller collectible and good conditions to $125 to $500 for larger near-mint and mints.

Lutz marbles, one of Runyan's favourites, have bands that appear to be gold, but are actually copper. "They are just beautiful and have gold flecks in concentrated bands with colours interspersed," she said.
A large mint Banded Lutz with a clear base can command $1,000 and a large good one may be worth $450.
An Onionskin Lutz, 1-5/8 inch to two inches in near-mint condition is valued at around $3,250, and a mint Ribbon Lutz of the same size is estimated at $3,000.
Peltier Glass made picture marbles featuring 12 King Syndicate comic characters. They are valued from $10 to $75, although many are too rare to value, according to the price guide.

Some of the company's Rainblo line of marbles are more commonly know as Bumblebee, Christmas Tree, Rebel, Ketchup & Mustard and Blue Zebra. A two-colour Rainblo has a value range of 25 cents for a collectible to $50 to $75 for near-mint or mints.
Marbles have been around for thousands of years and have been made of many different materials.
"It's the oldest international game we know of that is still being played today," said Runyan, noting that some were even found in King Tut's tomb.
